controls.name: integer_division_truncation
controls.description: Division uses Python's floor-division operator (//) instead of true division (/), a plausible slip when porting arithmetic logic from a language where '/' truncates. '7/2' returns 3.0 instead of 3.5. Everything else (precedence, associativity, unary minus, parentheses) is copied verbatim from the reference, isolating this single defect.

controls.name: right_associative_subtraction
controls.description: Re-introduces the real pre-Phase-35 defect this task was patched for: parse_expression/parse_term fold from the right instead of the left, so '10-2-3' evaluates as 10-(2-3)=11 instead of (10-2)-3=5, and '8/2/2' as 8/(2/2)=8 instead of 2. Unary minus handling is left correct (copied verbatim from the reference) so this control isolates only the associativity regression. The hidden suite's dedicated left-associativity tests must reject this.

controls.name: unary_minus_non_leading_crash
controls.description: Realistic partial fix for unary minus: parse_factor only special-cases a leading '+'/'-' when it is the very first token of the whole expression (self.pos == 0), instead of recognizing unary sign at every factor position. '-3+2' still works, but '1+-2', '6/-2', '2--3', and '3*(-2)' all raise ValueError because the parser reaches a bare '-' where it expects a number. Matches the prior real defect's 'unary-minus crashing' symptom.

controls.name: eval_based_implementation
controls.description: Task-specific, security-relevant near-miss: computes the answer with Python's eval() instead of a real parser, which the task prose explicitly forbids ('Do NOT use eval()') because handing attacker-influenced text to eval() is an arbitrary-code-execution risk, not a style nit. Python's own +,-,*,/ operators happen to share the same precedence, left-associativity, and unary-minus semantics the task specifies, so on every benign input the hidden suite exercises this produces byte-identical results to a correct parser. Expected reject: this is exactly the kind of spec-violating shortcut a naive or corner-cutting agent might submit. If the purely behavioral hidden suite accepts it, that is a genuine benchmark-integrity gap (nothing in the grading verifies the 'no eval()' constraint), not an authoring mistake.

controls.name: shunting_yard_rpn
controls.description: Structurally different but behaviorally equivalent correct implementation: a shunting-yard algorithm that converts tokens to RPN (with unary +/- represented as distinct, higher-precedence, right-associative pseudo-operators 'u+'/'u-' resolved via a two-stack shunting yard) and then evaluates the RPN with a single value stack. No recursive-descent grammar, no _Parser class, no eval(). Correctly preserves left-associativity for +-*/ and correct unary-minus semantics at every position (leading, after another operator, and inside parentheses).

findings.summary: A `_pytest/` package nested inside this task's editable subtree is not flagged as a protected-path violation, but empirical testing confirms this is NOT currently exploitable.
findings.detail: Injecting 'calckit/_pytest/__init__.py' (nested inside the editable package, not at the snapshot root) was NOT flagged as touching a protected path — but `python -m pytest` never adds the editable package directory itself to sys.path, so this nested `_pytest/` is only importable as `<package>._pytest`, never as the bare top-level `_pytest` the real pytest package needs; a controlled test confirms `import _pytest` still resolves to the real site-packages module. Recorded as a structural gap (no basename/suffix rule catches a directory named `_pytest`) that would only matter if this task ever lost its editable_paths allow-list, not as a live weakness today. See docs/agents/ORACLE.md.

limitations: Grading executes submitted/mutated code via LocalSandbox, which provides per-run workspace isolation and timeouts but NOT untrusted-agent security isolation (runner/afa_runner/sandbox.py's own module docstring). Every check in this report assumes the code being graded is trying to game the SCORE, not attack the HOST — see isolation.hidden_test_readability for a concrete, always-present consequence of that assumption.

Hidden-test readability during grading could not be ruled out (see the isolation.hidden_test_readability check) — this finding is deliberately excluded from the status precedence (afa_integrity.health) because it is a constant, documented property of the current LocalSandbox threat model, not something this specific task can fix.
